summary.text: For the candidate linear-recurrence solution, induction gives positivity and sufficient growth, while the defect \(D_n=b_{n+1}^2-b_nb_{n+2}\) satisfies \(D_{n+3}=4D_{n+1}+D_n\) and hence \(1\le D_n\le b_n\). Thus \(b_{n+1}^2=b_nb_{n+2}+D_n\) has exactly the remainder range forcing \(\lceil b_{n+1}^2/b_n\rceil-1=b_{n+2}\), so induction identifies the original nonlinear sequence with the candidate.

full_proof.text:
Let \((a_n)_{n\ge 0}\) be the sequence given by the original definition. Thus
\[
a_0=4,\qquad a_1=16,
\]
and, whenever the preceding terms are positive, \(a_{n+2}\) is the greatest integer \(c\) for which
\[
\frac{c}{a_{n+1}}<\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}.
\]
Equivalently,
\[
c<\frac{a_{n+1}^2}{a_n}.
\]
For any real number \(y\), the greatest integer strictly smaller than \(y\) is \(\lceil y\rceil-1\). Consequently the original recursion can be written
\[
a_{n+2}=\left\lceil\frac{a_{n+1}^2}{a_n}\right\rceil-1.
\tag{1}
\]
For positive integers \(P,Q\),
\[
\left\lceil\frac P Q\right\rceil
 =\left\lfloor\frac{P+Q-1}{Q}\right\rfloor,
\]
so (1) is also
\[
a_{n+2}=
\left\lfloor
\frac{a_{n+1}^2+a_n-1}{a_n}
\right\rfloor-1.
\tag{2}
\]
We shall prove that this nonlinear recursion agrees at every index with a linear recurrence.

Define an integer sequence \((b_n)_{n\ge0}\) by
\[
b_0=4,\qquad b_1=16,\qquad b_2=63,
\tag{3}
\]
and
\[
b_{n+3}=4b_{n+2}-b_n\qquad(n\ge0).
\tag{4}
\]
The first few terms are
\[
4,16,63,248,976,3841,\ldots,
\]
as expected. The main task is to prove that the rounding in (1) always gives exactly the next term of this sequence.

We first establish positivity and a useful growth estimate:
\[
b_n\ge1\quad\text{and}\quad b_{n+1}\ge3b_n
\qquad(n\ge0).
\tag{5}
\]
We prove both statements simultaneously by strong induction. They hold directly at the first three indices:
\[
4\ge1,\quad16\ge3\cdot4;
\]
\[
16\ge1,\quad63\ge3\cdot16;
\]
and
\[
63\ge1,\quad248=4\cdot63-4\ge3\cdot63.
\]
Now suppose the assertions have already been established through index \(m+2\). In particular,
\[
b_{m+1}\ge3b_m,
\qquad
b_{m+2}\ge3b_{m+1},
\qquad
b_m\ge1.
\]
Thus \(b_{m+2}\ge9b_m\), and (4) gives
\[
b_{m+3}=4b_{m+2}-b_m\ge36b_m-b_m=35b_m\ge1.
\]
For the growth inequality at this new index, the recurrence gives
\[
b_{m+4}=4b_{m+3}-b_{m+1}.
\]
It is therefore enough to show \(b_{m+3}\ge b_{m+1}\). But
\[
b_{m+3}=4b_{m+2}-b_m
 \ge12b_{m+1}-b_m.
\]
Since \(b_{m+1}\ge3b_m\), in particular \(b_m\le b_{m+1}\), so the right side is at least \(11b_{m+1}\), and hence certainly at least \(b_{m+1}\). Therefore
\[
b_{m+4}=4b_{m+3}-b_{m+1}\ge3b_{m+3}.
\]
This completes the strong induction and proves (5). In particular, every \(b_n\) is a positive integer.

We now introduce the quadratic discrepancy
\[
D_n=b_{n+1}^2-b_nb_{n+2}.
\tag{6}
\]
It measures the amount by which \(b_{n+1}^2\) exceeds \(b_nb_{n+2}\). We need two facts about this discrepancy: it is positive, and it is no greater than \(b_n\).

First, direct calculation gives
\[
D_0=16^2-4\cdot63=4,
\]
\[
D_1=63^2-16\cdot248=1,
\]
and
\[
D_2=248^2-63\cdot976=16.
\tag{7}
\]
The discrepancies themselves obey the recurrence
\[
D_{n+3}=4D_{n+1}+D_n.
\tag{8}
\]
To see this, use (4) successively to write
\[
b_{n+3}=4b_{n+2}-b_n,
\]
\[
b_{n+4}=4b_{n+3}-b_{n+1},
\]
and
\[
b_{n+5}=4b_{n+4}-b_{n+2}.
\]
Substituting these expressions into
\[
D_{n+3}=b_{n+4}^2-b_{n+3}b_{n+5}
\]
and expanding and collecting terms gives
\[
D_{n+3}
 =4\bigl(b_{n+2}^2-b_{n+1}b_{n+3}\bigr)
  +\bigl(b_{n+1}^2-b_nb_{n+2}\bigr)
 =4D_{n+1}+D_n,
\]
which proves (8).

It follows at once by strong induction from (7) and (8) that
\[
D_n\ge1\qquad(n\ge0).
\tag{9}
\]
Indeed, this is true for \(n=0,1,2\); and if it is true at the required earlier indices, then
\[
D_{m+3}=4D_{m+1}+D_m\ge4\cdot1+1\ge1.
\]

We next prove the upper bound
\[
D_n\le b_n\qquad(n\ge0).
\tag{10}
\]
The initial cases follow from (3) and (7):
\[
D_0=4\le4=b_0,
\qquad
D_1=1\le16=b_1,
\qquad
D_2=16\le63=b_2.
\]
Suppose inductively that
\[
D_m\le b_m,
\qquad
D_{m+1}\le b_{m+1}.
\]
By (8),
\[
D_{m+3}=4D_{m+1}+D_m
 \le4b_{m+1}+b_m.
\tag{11}
\]
On the other hand, the growth inequalities (5) give
\[
b_m\le b_{m+1}
\quad\text{and}\quad
b_{m+2}\ge3b_{m+1}.
\]
Consequently
\[
4b_{m+1}+2b_m
 \le6b_{m+1}
 \le12b_{m+1}
 \le4b_{m+2}.
\]
After moving one copy of \(b_m\) to the other side, this says
\[
4b_{m+1}+b_m\le4b_{m+2}-b_m=b_{m+3}.
\tag{12}
\]
Combining (11) and (12) gives \(D_{m+3}\le b_{m+3}\). Strong induction therefore proves (10).

We have thus established the crucial interval
\[
1\le D_n\le b_n
\qquad(n\ge0).
\tag{13}
\]
By the definition (6), we also have the exact identity
\[
b_{n+1}^2=b_nb_{n+2}+D_n.
\tag{14}
\]
We now use (13) and (14) to show that the ceiling recursion (1) selects \(b_{n+2}\) exactly.

We prove \(a_n=b_n\) for all \(n\) by strong induction. The first two values agree by definition:
\[
a_0=4=b_0,
\qquad
 a_1=16=b_1.
\]
Suppose that the equality is already known at indices \(k\) and \(k+1\). Set
\[
Q=b_k,
\qquad P=b_{k+1},
\qquad R=b_{k+2},
\qquad D=D_k.
\]
All of \(P,Q,R\) are positive, and (13) says
\[
1\le D\le Q.
\tag{15}
\]
Equation (14) becomes
\[
P^2=QR+D.
\tag{16}
\]
Using the integer form (2) of the original recursion and the induction hypothesis, we obtain
\[
a_{k+2}
 =\left\lfloor\frac{P^2+Q-1}{Q}\right\rfloor-1.
\tag{17}
\]
By (16), the numerator in (17) has the exact decomposition
\[
P^2+Q-1
 =QR+D+Q-1
 =Q(R+1)+(D-1).
\tag{18}
\]
The bounds (15) imply
\[
0\le D-1<Q.
\]
Thus (18) is the Euclidean division of the numerator by \(Q\), with quotient \(R+1\) and remainder \(D-1\). Hence
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{P^2+Q-1}{Q}\right\rfloor=R+1.
\]
Substitution into (17) yields
\[
a_{k+2}=R=b_{k+2}.
\]
This completes the strong induction. Therefore
\[
a_n=b_n\qquad\text{for every }n\ge0.
\tag{19}
\]
In particular, because the \(b_n\) are positive, this also confirms at every stage that the ratios in the original definition have positive denominators.

Combining (19) with (3) and (4), the sequence from the original definition satisfies
\[
a_0=4,
\qquad a_1=16,
\qquad a_2=63,
\]
and, for every \(n\ge3\),
\[
a_n=4a_{n-1}-a_{n-3}.
\tag{20}
\]
The right side is positive by the preceding argument, so (20) is an equality of ordinary nonnegative integers; no truncation issue arises in the subtraction.

Finally, let
\[
A(x)=\sum_{n\ge0}a_nx^n
\]
be the ordinary generating function, interpreted as a formal power series. Multiplying by \(1-4x+x^3\), the coefficient of \(x^n\) for every \(n\ge3\) is
\[
a_n-4a_{n-1}+a_{n-3},
\]
which vanishes by (20). The three remaining coefficients are
\[
[x^0]:(a_0)=4,
\]
\[
[x^1]:(a_1-4a_0)=16-4\cdot4=0,
\]
and
\[
[x^2]:(a_2-4a_1)=63-4\cdot16=-1.
\]
Therefore
\[
(1-4x+x^3)A(x)=4-x^2,
\]
and hence
\[
\boxed{A(x)=\frac{4-x^2}{1-4x+x^3}}.
\]
This proves the conjectured generating function for the sequence defined by the original consecutive-ratio extremal rule.
